# Finance flagged our CI bill and I cannot tell which half of Marco's plan is real

## Problem Description

We went cross-platform on `paperclip` in July and our CI spend went from $612 in
June to $2,336 in August. Finance has asked for it down by the end of the month.
The August usage export from the billing page is attached, along with the
workflow.

Marco has written the plan and wants to merge it tomorrow. I would like a second
opinion first, because I am not a CI person and I cannot tell which of his four
items are real savings and which are him being confident. In his words:

1. "Leave the matrix alone. It already stops the whole thing the moment one job
   fails, which is the single biggest thing keeping this bill from being worse. I
   want that written into the file explicitly so nobody 'fixes' it later."
2. "Shard the suite four ways. It takes eleven minutes; four shards takes about
   three; so we pay roughly a quarter of what we pay now for the same tests."
3. "Delete the macOS leg. Look at the export - it is the expensive one by a
   mile, and Linux and Windows between them cover everything a user can hit."
4. "Take Node 20 off the pull-request trigger and run it once a night instead.
   Pull requests keep Node 22 only."

Two things I know that are not in his write-up. Our desktop build ships a macOS
app. And when I asked around, two of the three release blockers we caught last
quarter were found by the macOS leg and by nothing else - they are listed at the
bottom of the export.

Get the bill down. Tell me plainly which of the four to approve and which not,
with the reason in each case, and what you did instead.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`, splitting it into more than one workflow
   file if that is what your plan needs.
2. Write `docs/ci-cost-plan.md`: a verdict on each of Marco's four items with the
   reason, the jobs-per-run count before and after for each trigger, and an
   estimate of the monthly billable minutes your plan removes, worked from the
   attached export.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`, splitting it into more than one workflow
   file if that is what your plan needs.
2. Write `docs/ci-cost-plan.md`: a verdict on each of Marco's four items with the
   reason, the jobs-per-run count before and after for each trigger, and an
   estimate of the monthly billable minutes your plan removes, worked from the
   attached export.
assertions: Item 1 MUST be refused and the matrix MUST end up carrying an explicit fail-fast: false. Endorsing item 1, writing fail-fast: true, or leaving the matrix at its default so it keeps cancelling siblings, each scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks need the refusal plus the reason - a failure on one platform cancels the legs that have not reported, so the run says nothing about the other platforms and the money already spent on them buys nothing - and an acknowledgement that this change costs minutes which the rest of the plan has to cover. Setting it correctly while leaving item 1 unanswered in the document scores at most half.

Item 2's arithmetic MUST be corrected: sharding divides elapsed time, not billed time, and on this matrix it multiplies the job count so each shard pays its own checkout and install on top. Repeating or endorsing the claim that four shards cost roughly a quarter scores zero for this criterion, and so does applying four-way sharding across the full operating-system and runtime matrix, which raises the bill the plan was written to lower. Accepting sharding narrowly for elapsed time on one tier while stating plainly that it saves no money scores full marks; refusing it outright with the right reason also scores full marks.

The plan addresses the 11 jobs the platform killed at six hours - a job-level time limit short enough to stop a hung job burning a full day of the most expensive runner, plus a note that a suite whose longest honest run is 14 minutes should never approach it. Not mentioning them at all scores zero: they are on the ten-times runner and are worth more than the whole Linux line of the export, and no other item in Marco's plan touches them.

A concurrency group is added so that when a newer commit lands on the same branch the older run is cancelled rather than finishing, which is the 148 runs in the export. Omitting it scores zero. A group keyed so that every branch shares one lane, so that unrelated branches cancel each other, scores at most half.

Item 3 MUST be refused - two of the three Q2 release blockers were found on macOS and by nothing else, and the product ships a macOS app. Deleting the macOS leg outright scores zero. Keeping it on every pull request unchanged, with no answer for the fact that it is 79% of the bill, scores at most half: the saving has to come from running it less often rather than from not running it.

Item 4 is approved and implemented, and more generally the plan runs a small matrix on pull requests and the wider one on merges or on a schedule, with the jobs-per-run count given for each trigger as the output specification asks. Refusing all four of Marco's items scores zero here - one of them is right, and an answer that rejects the lot has failed in the opposite direction from an answer that accepts the lot.

The estimate in docs/ci-cost-plan.md applies the per-runner multipliers from the export, so a macOS minute is not counted as equal to a Linux minute. A plan that totals or ranks its savings in raw runner minutes scores zero - it is the specific error that makes the Windows and macOS legs look comparable when one costs five times the other.
The rewritten workflow file or files and docs/ci-cost-plan.md all exist, and the document carries a separate verdict on each of Marco's four items rather than one verdict on the plan as a whole.

# Security review flagged the tokens someone pasted into our workflow

## Problem Description

`wavelet-cli` is our open-source CLI. Public repo, 31 forks, MIT, and we take a
steady trickle of outside contributions. Last week's security review flagged the
test workflow; the finding is attached along with the workflow itself and the
`git log` for that file.

The short version: when Tom set up the publish step in July he pasted the npm
token and our Slack webhook straight into the YAML. They have been sitting in a
public repository for seven weeks. I need this cleaned up today and I need to be
able to tell the reviewer on Friday exactly what we did, in writing, without a
second round.

Tom has written up what he wants to do this afternoon. He is the one who got us
here and he has been thorough since, so I am inclined to say yes, but I want a
second opinion first. His four items:

1. Every value under an `env:` key moves into repository secrets. The token, the
   webhook, the database URL, the Postgres password, `CI`, the timezone, all of
   it. Nothing readable stays in that file.
2. Force-push `main` with the token line deleted, so it is out of the history and
   we are back to clean.
3. Switch the `on: pull_request` trigger to `on: pull_request_target`. This is
   the one he is proudest of, because it also closes issue #488, attached -
   outside contributors have not been able to get a green run for two weeks,
   which is embarrassing on a project that asks for contributions. He has tried
   it on his own fork and the run comes back green.
4. Add a `permissions:` block at the top of the file so the automatic token the
   workflow gets is read-only unless a job asks for more.

Tell me which of those four to let him do, do the parts that should be done, and
be specific about anything else the reviewer will want from us - I would rather
hear it now than on Friday.

One constraint. The integration job runs against a throwaway Postgres container
that GitHub creates for the duration of the job and destroys with it; there is no
database of ours behind it, and it has to still work when you are done.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`. The integration job must still be able
   to reach its database, and `npm publish` on `main` must still be able to
   authenticate against the registry.
2. Write `docs/secret-remediation.md`: a verdict on each of Tom's four items with
   the reason, a row for every value currently sitting under an `env:` key in
   that workflow with a verdict for each one, what we are doing about issue #488,
   and the steps we owe the reviewer by Friday.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`. The integration job must still be able
   to reach its database, and `npm publish` on `main` must still be able to
   authenticate against the registry.
2. Write `docs/secret-remediation.md`: a verdict on each of Tom's four items with
   the reason, a row for every value currently sitting under an `env:` key in
   that workflow with a verdict for each one, what we are doing about issue #488,
   and the steps we owe the reviewer by Friday.
assertions: Item 3 MUST be refused. Changing `on: pull_request` to a trigger that runs in the base repository's context with the repository's secrets and a writable token, while checking out and running a contributor's branch, scores zero for this criterion regardless of everything else - implementing it, or endorsing it in the document while not implementing it, both score zero. Full marks need the refusal, the reason, and an actual answer for issue #488: the dashboard step stops blocking pull requests that come from forks (skipped for them, or made non-blocking), and the publish credential is placed where a fork run never needs it. Refusing the trigger change but leaving #488 unanswered scores at most half; the contributor is two weeks in and the prompt asks what we are doing about it.

The npm token and the Slack webhook are referenced through secrets and no literal credential is left in the YAML; leaving either literal in place scores zero. Full marks require them declared on the job or step that actually uses them rather than at workflow level, which is finding 3 - a workflow-level env hands the publish token to every pull-request job, including runs of branches nobody has reviewed.

The answer states that the npm token and the Slack webhook must both be revoked and reissued, and says why relocation cannot substitute: the values were public for seven weeks and the file's history exists in 31 forks and in every clone taken since July. An answer that only moves the values into secrets scores zero here. Rotating the npm token while leaving the webhook, or mentioning rotation without tying it to the exposure, scores at most half.

CI, TZ, the service container's POSTGRES_PASSWORD and the localhost DATABASE_URL MUST NOT be moved into repository secrets. Moving all of them scores zero; moving some of them scores at most half. Full marks need the reason in docs/secret-remediation.md - the container is created and destroyed with the job and is reachable only from inside it, so these are configuration, and putting configuration behind secrets costs reviewability and log legibility and buys nothing.

After the change `npm publish` on main can still authenticate: the runtime setup step configures the registry and the token is exposed under the environment variable name the registry client actually reads, or an equivalent explicit registry-config step is added. Simply renaming the literal into a secrets reference under the old variable name, with nothing configuring the registry, scores zero - the next release fails on authentication and nobody finds out until then. Getting the variable name right but not configuring the registry scores at most half.

The 'Label the run' step MUST NOT keep the pull-request title expanded directly into its `run:` command. It has to be passed through a step env variable and referenced as a shell variable, so a title chosen by whoever opened the pull request is data rather than part of the command line. Leaving the expansion in the command scores zero. Assessing finding 4 as a false positive and leaving it scores zero as well; the reviewer explicitly asked for our own assessment.

Item 2 is refused, or at minimum stated to be irrelevant to the exposure. Presenting deletion of the line, a history rewrite or a force-push as what puts the credential beyond reach scores zero - the forks and clones keep their copies either way, and that answer to the reviewer would be wrong.

Item 4 is approved and implemented: an explicit permissions block restricting the automatic token, with any job that needs more asking for it. Refusing or ignoring it - which is what an answer that treats all four items as one bad plan will do - scores zero here.

Whatever is done to the Postgres password and the connection string keeps the two consistent, so the integration job can still authenticate. Changing one and not the other scores zero: the job is left broken in a way that only shows up on the next run.

docs/secret-remediation.md carries a verdict on each of Tom's four items separately and a row per value currently under an env: key - CI, TZ, NPM_TOKEN, SLACK_WEBHOOK, DASHBOARD_TOKEN, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, DATABASE_URL. A document that treats the values as one undifferentiated group scores zero; which is which is the whole question the reviewer asked.

# Our summary job reports "0 tests, 0 failures" on a run where 900 tests ran

## Problem Description

`paper-trail` has a 900-test suite. It used to run in one job and took 28
minutes, which nobody could live with, so last month I split it across four
shards and we are down to about 8. I am not giving that back.

At the same time I added a `summary` job that runs `scripts/summarize-junit.mjs`
over the JUnit the shards write, so a reviewer gets one line on the PR instead of
four collapsed job logs. Since I bumped the upload and download actions to v4 in
August that line has said the same thing on every run: `0 tests, 0 failures`. Run
4612 is attached - four green shards, 900 tests actually executed, a summary job
that found nothing and reported success anyway.

Run 4620 is the one that actually hurt. Two shards red, four failing tests
between them, and the summary job says `skipped`. So on a green run we publish a
line that is a lie, and on a red run we publish nothing at all. Somebody read
that green line last Thursday and approved on the strength of it.

Jules has had a look. He thinks the four uploads are racing each other and
clobbering the result, and says the fix is to go back to the way it worked before
the version bump - point all four shard uploads at one artifact name, so there is
a single artifact and nothing left to race. He also wants `continue-on-error:
true` on the upload step, so that a shard which has trouble uploading does not
take the whole build down with it. That is two small edits, he has been right
about this kind of thing before, and I would like it done today unless you can
tell me why not.

`scripts/summarize-junit.mjs` is off limits. The nightly workflow and the release
job both call it, the platform team owns it, and a change there needs their
review and a week I do not have. Whatever the fix is, it has to be on our side of
that line.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`. Keep four shards.
2. Write `docs/ci-shard-summary.md`: why the summary reads zero on a run where
   900 tests passed, what you did with each of Jules's two suggestions and why,
   and what a reviewer will see on a run where a shard goes red.
3. Leave `scripts/summarize-junit.mjs`, `test/` and `src/` exactly as they are.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`. Keep four shards.
2. Write `docs/ci-shard-summary.md`: why the summary reads zero on a run where
   900 tests passed, what you did with each of Jules's two suggestions and why,
   and what a reviewer will see on a run where a shard goes red.
3. Leave `scripts/summarize-junit.mjs`, `test/` and `src/` exactly as they are.
assertions: Jules's revert MUST NOT be implemented: the four shards must keep distinct artifact names. Pointing them at a single shared name scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest, because artifact names must be unique within a run at the action version in use and the second, third and fourth uploads fail on the conflict - three shards' results lost, with the summary reporting whichever one arrived first as though it were the run. Full marks need the refusal plus the reason recorded in docs/ci-shard-summary.md, not merely leaving the names as they are. Rejecting it in the YAML while saying nothing about it in the document scores at most half; the requester asked for it explicitly and will otherwise re-raise it.

The summary job's download is changed so the shard XML files end up directly in the directory handed to the script - by merging the downloaded artifacts into one directory, with or without a name pattern, or by downloading each artifact by name into that one directory. Leaving the download at its default, which gives each artifact its own subdirectory and leaves the top level empty, scores zero: run 4612 repeats exactly and the summary keeps reporting a run it never read.

The per-shard result files must be distinguishable once they are in one directory - the shard index in the JUnit filename the reporter writes, or an equivalent arrangement. Four files all called junit.xml arriving in a single directory scores zero, because three of them are lost and the summary line reports about a quarter of the suite while looking entirely healthy. Making the artifact names distinct but leaving the filename inside each one identical does not satisfy this.

The shard upload step MUST NOT be given continue-on-error, which is Jules's second suggestion and turns a shard whose results never arrived into a silent absence the summary cannot distinguish from a shard that passed; that scores zero here. The upload also needs an explicit always-run condition so that a shard whose tests failed uploads its JUnit at all - run 4620 shows junit-1 and junit-3 missing from the artifact list for exactly that reason. Adding the condition but also adding continue-on-error still scores zero.

The summary job carries an explicit always-run condition alongside its needs: dependency, so it is not skipped when a shard fails. Leaving run 4620's behaviour in place scores zero. Full marks also require that the summary job's own result still reflects a red run rather than reporting success over failing shards.

docs/ci-shard-summary.md says why a green run summarised as zero: the downloaded artifacts were in per-artifact subdirectories and the script reads only the top level of the directory it is given. A document that repeats the requester's or Jules's theory - that the uploads were racing, or that something wiped the directory - scores zero even if the YAML happens to be right.

scripts/summarize-junit.mjs MUST NOT be modified, including making it walk subdirectories, since two other workflows call it and the prompt puts it out of scope. Editing it scores zero here even though it would make the symptom go away.

The four-shard matrix stays. Collapsing it back into one job so the results and the summary share a workspace scores zero: it solves the handoff by giving back the 28-minute suite the split was done to escape.
A rewritten .github/workflows/test.yml and docs/ci-shard-summary.md both exist, and the document addresses both of Jules's suggestions separately rather than as one.

# A run with six failing tests posted a green check and merged

## Problem Description

`ledger-api` is a small Node service. Its PR job runs two suites. The unit suite
is ours. The contract suite belongs to the payments team and is the only reason
they let us ship without a manual sign-off, and their standing condition is that
it reports on every single run - including runs where our unit suite has already
fallen over. That condition is not up for renegotiation and I would rather you
told me a change is impossible than quietly traded it away.

Back in August the problem was artifacts. The moment the suite went red, the
JUnit file and the debug logs were not in the run's artifact list, so whoever got
paged had nothing to open. Run 8790 is the shape of it and it cost us an evening.
Priya rewrote the job on 21 Aug and that part genuinely worked - every step runs
now, on every run, and for the first time I can predict what I will get out of a
red build.

Then run 9042 happened, and it is attached. Six failing tests, a green check, and
the PR merged forty minutes later by someone who had no reason to doubt it. The
last step in that job is called "Fail the job if anything failed", and the log
says it was skipped. That step exists for precisely this run and precisely this
merge and it did not execute, and I cannot work out why from staring at the YAML.

What I want out of this: a red suite produces a red check, and the artifacts and
the coverage push keep happening on red runs, because losing those is what we
were fixing in the first place. While you are in there I also want a written
position on every step in that job - which of them should be running after a red
suite and which should not. I have never seen that written down and after 9042 I
do not trust my own read of it.

Do not touch `.github/workflows/lint.yml`; another team owns that file and we
have a standing agreement not to edit each other's workflows. Do not change what
either suite asserts - if a test is wrong that is a separate conversation.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`.
2. Write `docs/ci-step-policy.md`: a row per step of the `test` job saying
   whether that step runs after a red suite and why, plus what the check on run
   9042 would have reported once your change is in.
3. Leave `.github/workflows/lint.yml`, `test/`, `contract/` and `src/` exactly as
   they are.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/test.yml`.
2. Write `docs/ci-step-policy.md`: a row per step of the `test` job saying
   whether that step runs after a red suite and why, plus what the check on run
   9042 would have reported once your change is in.
3. Leave `.github/workflows/lint.yml`, `test/`, `contract/` and `src/` exactly as
   they are.
assertions: A failing suite must make the job fail. Two mechanisms are acceptable: keep continue-on-error on the suite steps and gate the job on steps.unit.outcome and steps.contract.outcome, or drop continue-on-error and give the contract step an explicit always-run condition so it still executes. What MUST NOT survive is if: failure() - or any other test of job status, such as job.status == 'failure' - as the gate while a continue-on-error step precedes it, because that is the condition that was skipped in run 9042. Leaving it scores zero for this criterion regardless of everything else in the answer. Gating on only one of the two suites, so the other can fail silently, scores at most half.

'Push preview image' and 'Update the :latest tag' MUST NOT keep an always-run condition - if: always(), if: !cancelled(), if: success() || failure() - and MUST NOT be given continue-on-error instead. Either scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks need both left conditional on the suites having passed, plus the reason recorded in docs/ci-step-policy.md: a step that pushes an image consumers pull, or moves a floating tag onto the commit, is not a reporting step and does not belong on the failure path. Making them conditional with no reasoning written down scores at most half.

The JUnit and debug-log upload and the coverage push both keep an explicit always-run condition, so run 8790's outcome - no artifacts on exactly the runs anyone wants - cannot recur. Stripping the condition from either of them scores zero here, which is the trap in tidying the whole block the same way in the other direction.

A failure in the unit suite MUST NOT prevent the contract suite from running. A workflow in which a red unit suite skips the contract step scores zero whatever mechanism was used to make the check honest - that is run 8790's behaviour and the prompt states payments will not accept it. Removing continue-on-error from the unit step without putting an always-run condition on the contract step is the specific way this is lost.

docs/ci-step-policy.md gives a row per step of the test job with whether it runs after a red suite and why, and states what run 9042 would have reported once the change is in: a failing check, with the artifacts and coverage still published and the two registry steps skipped. A single verdict for the whole job scores zero; omitting the run 9042 restatement scores at most half.
The separately owned .github/workflows/lint.yml MUST NOT be modified, merged into test.yml, or reformatted. Any change to it scores zero here, including a change that is an improvement.
No file under test/, contract/ or src/ is edited, skipped or deleted. Making the check honest by changing what the suites assert scores zero here.

# Windows users keep hitting a crash our CI has never once reproduced

## Problem Description

`acme-sync` is a CLI we publish to npm. It is installed on Linux, macOS and
Windows, and roughly a third of our installs are Windows. Our CI has only ever
run on Linux.

Support ticket 3318 is the third Windows crash this quarter and it is attached. A
customer on Windows 11 gets `ENOENT: no such file or directory` for a path that
has a forward slash in the middle of it and backslashes at both ends. Our suite
is 100% green on every run and has been for months.

Dan wants this done this week and his plan is three lines long:

1. Put the first job on all three operating systems - ubuntu plus macos plus
   windows, Node 20 and 22. "If it runs everywhere we stop shipping Windows
   bugs."
2. Put the second job, the one that talks to Postgres, on all three as well,
   because in his words the database-backed tests are the ones that hammer the
   file paths hardest.
3. Run every job inside the `node:22-bookworm` image, so all three operating
   systems get a byte-identical environment and we stop chasing differences
   between runners instead of differences in our own code.

We have already tried parts of this twice and both logs are attached. Run 2291 in
June added the three operating systems and was reverted the next morning. Run
2402 in July was a second attempt with a change to the step that runs
`scripts/verify.sh`, and it was reverted too. Nobody left on the team can tell me
whether we keep failing because the idea is wrong or because we keep executing it
badly, and that is the part I need settled.

What I want out of this is the Windows signal we have never had, and whatever you
write has to run on the first try - after a third revert people here will stop
believing this is fixable at all. If a piece of Dan's plan cannot work, I would
much rather be told now, with the reason, than find out from a red main branch.

## Output Specification

1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.
2. Change whatever files are needed so the suite is green on all three operating
   systems rather than only on Linux.
3. Write `docs/os-coverage-plan.md`: what runs on which operating systems, a
   verdict on each of Dan's three items with the technical reason for it, and
   what actually happened in runs 2291 and 2402.
evals.expected_output:
1. Rewrite `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.
2. Change whatever files are needed so the suite is green on all three operating
   systems rather than only on Linux.
3. Write `docs/os-coverage-plan.md`: what runs on which operating systems, a
   verdict on each of Dan's three items with the technical reason for it, and
   what actually happened in runs 2291 and 2402.
assertions: Items 2 and 3 MUST both be refused. No services: block may appear in a job that runs on macOS or Windows, and no job container may be introduced at all on this matrix. Implementing either scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require both refusals in docs/os-coverage-plan.md with the technical reason - service containers and job containers need a Linux runner - plus, for item 3, the second reason that an identical Linux container on every runner would remove the platform differences the exercise exists to detect, and plus what is offered instead for the database job. Refusing one of the two and accepting the other scores at most half; silently leaving the database job on Linux without telling Dan why also scores at most half, because he asked for it explicitly and will re-open it.

Two things are needed and run 2402 shows that the first alone is not enough. The step invoking ./scripts/verify.sh gets an explicit bash shell (or an equivalent per-operating-system arrangement), and the repository's line-ending configuration is changed so shell scripts are checked out with LF on every platform rather than the platform's native ending. Doing neither scores zero. Doing only the shell change scores at most half - that is precisely run 2402, which failed on the carriage return. Stripping carriage returns inside the workflow, with a conversion step or a sed, instead of fixing how the repository checks the file out, also scores at most half: the next script added has the same problem and every Windows developer still gets the broken copy.

src/config.mjs stops building paths by string concatenation and joins them with the platform-aware path API, so ticket 3318's mixed-separator path cannot be produced. Editing only the workflow and leaving config.mjs as it is scores zero - no amount of CI coverage fixes a binary already on customers' machines.
